headings: # Borrow the Adult Before You Can Be the Adult
## Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care

rows.label: Your updated paragraph (13:10 UTC), word for word; the old first half stays above it (question 93.3)
rows.start: And even (or especially) when I am suffering

beside.label: The paragraph it came from
beside.text: That may sound like a silly, quirky waste of time to some folks. But what I notice is that saying thank you for every little thing, whenever I remember to, is not about imposing some kind of “spiritual discipline.” It is directly reconnecting me to something pure and sacred. And even (or especially) when I am suffering, I try to remember to be grateful for that also, because if not for suffering, I would not even think about how much I have enjoyed not suffering as much, and how much it will help me to develop more compassion, wisdom, and gratitude in future. It connects me with the plight of the countless other beings suffering at that very moment, authentically bringing up a wellspring of compassion in my heart for all of us. And I see clearly that it is my inner child who is feeling this pain, and what an honor it is that I can be there for him.

rows.label: Your updated paragraph (13:10 UTC), word for word (questions 93.1 and 93.2)
rows.start: Of course, that’s not to say you should not try to suffer

beside.label: What it replaced
beside.text: Of course, that’s not to say you should not try to suffer less, nor does gratitude for difficulties justify staying with an abuser. The point of life, according to every spiritual tradition and religion, I think, is to suffer less, which first requires us to understand the cause of suffering, and what real suffering and real happiness are. If you, like Biggie Smalls, have come to understand that having money is not real happiness, that’s a big deal! That’s something to be grateful for. Because getting what you want is an endless loop, and it doesn’t lead to being content with less. When you can see that less is more, at a deeper level, that’s where the real gratitude flourishes.

headings: # Sometimes There Isn't a Clear Child Yet

rows.label: New, after your memoir paragraph (PGQ-046, its first half)
rows.start: What I found, once I started cultivating my own happiness

beside.label: PGQ-046's teaching point (innerSignalGraph queue, your amendment of 2026-10-22)
beside.text: Feeling guilty about being happy while others suffer may be a belonging bargain. The author describes finding he could better help others toward happiness after beginning to cultivate his own. Explore the possibility that caring for one's wellbeing can expand what one gives, without claiming unhappy people cannot help. Some companions may genuinely resent another person's growth; a friend may withdraw. Take the social loss seriously, check real behavior and duties rather than presuming envy, and support compassionate limits instead of a requirement to stay unhappy.

rows.label: P5 (rewritten: the Guide's idea as one spoken line)
rows.start: Once a need does show, after all that hiding
source: The opposite trap is forced adulthood: perfect discipline, n

beside.label: What it replaced (Low 42 in rounds 4 and 5)
beside.text: Once a need does show, after all that hiding, it's okay to want a lot of closeness. So then someone you love goes for a walk alone, and you've texted "hello??" before they're at the corner. When they get back, you sulk all night. Wanting them close is fine! The texts and the sulking aren't, and the Guide can help you find something that leaves room for both of you, like a hug at the door and a "see you in an hour." But hear your little one out first. I think it just wants to know they're coming back.

headings: # When One Life Has Ended and the Next Hasn’t Begun

rows.label: P1 (rewritten: no chain of steps after the list)
rows.start: Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends
source: The inner child often becomes loudest in the gap after one l

beside.label: What it replaced (Low 14 and Low 61 in round 5)
beside.text: Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, your youngest moving out. So can leaving a family or community, or staying in one on new terms. A therapist or helper stepping back can do it too, after you've grown a lot. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state a bardo. You don't have to buy what it teaches about death and rebirth to use the everyday part: endings leave a stretch where the old you is gone and the new one hasn't shown up.

rows.label: P7 (rewritten: its last sentence)
rows.start: And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters

beside.label: What it replaced (Low 9 and Low 30 in round 5)
beside.text: And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... At some point it's a maze, with a little one somewhere in the middle of it. A gentle practitioner can walk you through it fine. With others, people seem to come out more fragmented than they went in. Having a big institute with certifications behind it doesn't make a model any truer or safer.
